item.title: Scaling an autonomous agent from one team to fifty: A serverless-to-container decision framework
item.dc:creator: Rashmi Erande
item.description:
QA teams shipping complex products generate test failures around the clock. Every failure needs a bug ticket with steps, screenshots,

The post Scaling an autonomous agent from one team to fifty: A serverless-to-container decision framework appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
QA teams shipping complex products generate test failures around the clock. Every failure needs a bug ticket with steps, screenshots, repro rates, and regression labels. The manual process takes 10-15 minutes per failure. Multiply that by 30+ failures per week across a team, and you have burned an entire engineering day on documentation that should be automatic.

I built a system to eliminate this entirely. Not a dashboard. Not a notification bot. An autonomous agent that observes test results, makes judgment calls – is this a new bug, a duplicate, or a regression? And takes action without human intervention. It files structured bugs, attaches screenshots, calculates repro rates, detects regressions build-over-build, and notifies the right people. The team just marks FAIL and moves on.

The system runs on Lambda today. It works perfectly for one team. But what happens when other teams want it? What happens when you need to serve 10, 50, or 100 teams? That’s where the architectural decisions get interesting – not because Lambda fails, but because the workload characteristics shift into territory where a different tool becomes the better fit.

What I built (and why it works)

The architecture is elegant: an EventBridge rule triggers a Lambda function every 15 minutes. The function polls the test management API, processes failures through a decision engine (dedup check against DynamoDB, regression detection against previous build results), and files bugs via the JIRA API. Total infrastructure cost: under $5/month.

Lambda was the correct choice here for three reasons:

  1. Zero operational overhead: No servers, no scaling config, no patching. Deploy and forget.
  2. Cost proportional to usage: One team generates ~200 invocations/month. At Lambda pricing, this is effectively free.
  3. Fast iteration: The decision engine went through 20+ revisions in the first month. Lambda’s deployment model let me ship changes in seconds.

Within weeks of deploying, the system filed more complete and consistent bugs than the team had ever produced manually. Zero missed failures. Regressions caught in minutes instead of days. Status interruptions to QA dropped to zero because anyone could query the system directly via Slack. 8-10 hours per week saved.

Other teams have noticed. “Can we have that?” is a recurring question. The answer seems simple – deploy another instance per team. But at scale, the workload characteristics change in ways that shift the architectural decision.

The scaling decision

Lambda handles single-tenant agentic workloads beautifully. The challenge at multi-tenant scale isn’t that Lambda can’t do it; it’s that the workload characteristics shift:

From stateless events to long-running context: A single team’s poll cycle finishes in seconds. But cross-project correlation – “is this the same failure pattern we’re seeing across three teams?” requires analyzing hundreds of results and their relationships in a single pass. That’s a fundamentally different compute profile.

From isolated invocations to shared resource contention: When 50 functions trigger on the same EventBridge schedule, they all hit TestRail and JIRA APIs simultaneously. You need centralized rate limiting, connection pooling, and backpressure – patterns that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure.

From single-team to multi-tenant isolation: Each team needs guaranteed resources, network boundaries, and scoped credentials. The isolation model becomes as important as the compute model.

Lambda’s recent launches address many of these individually – Managed Instances solve connection persistence, Durable Functions break the 15-minute ceiling for long-running workflows, and Tenant Isolation provides native tenant boundaries. For many multi-tenant workloads, these capabilities narrow the gap significantly.

But for this specific workload – long-running agents that need persistent connections, cross-tenant analysis, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation simultaneously- the decision framework points toward a container-native execution model with serverless-like operations. That’s where EKS Auto Mode fits.

The decision framework

This led me to build a simple decision rubric – not Lambda vs. containers, but which characteristics does your workload actually exhibit?

“The deciding factor for my workload: I need all of the right-column characteristics simultaneously. Together, they compose more naturally in a container-native environment.”

The deciding factor for my workload: I need all of the right-column characteristics simultaneously. Cross-team pattern detection requires a shared analysis context. ML-based bug classification requires burst GPU. Per-team isolation requires namespace-level boundaries. Centralized rate limiting requires a persistent shared service. Each of these is individually solvable in Lambda. Together, they compose more naturally in a container-native environment.

What unlocks at scale: cross-team intelligence

The most interesting architectural capability that emerges at multi-tenant scale isn’t per-team automation – it’s cross-team pattern detection. This is what makes the scaling exercise worthwhile.

Cross-team failure correlation

When 50 teams run their test suites independently, failures appear isolated. But patterns emerge across teams that no single team can see:

  • Three teams report navigation failures on the same firmware build → systemic regression, not three independent bugs
  • Test failures correlate with deployment timing across unrelated services → infrastructure issue, not product bugs
  • Identical error signatures across teams with different test suites → shared dependency failure

This requires an analysis engine that can hold context from all teams simultaneously – comparing fingerprints, correlating timestamps, and identifying shared root causes. That’s a persistent, long-running workload with access to cross-tenant state. It runs naturally as a shared service in a platform namespace, consuming events from all tenant agents.

ML-based bug classification

Once you have enough historical data (thousands of bugs filed across teams), patterns become classifiable:

  • Auto-assign bugs to the correct component owner based on failure signature
  • Predict severity based on failure characteristics (crash vs. degraded behavior vs. cosmetic)
  • Suggest related bugs for investigation (“this looks like the same root cause as PROJ-4521”)
  • Detect anomalous failure rates before they become incident-scale

This inference workload is bursty – you need GPU when bugs arrive, not 24/7. A GPU NodePool that scales to zero when idle and provisions g5 instances only during inference keeps costs proportional to actual usage. The same pod that files a bug can synchronously call the classification service, get a component assignment, and include it in the ticket – all within the same request path.

Queryable knowledge base via Slack

The agent isn’t just an automation – it becomes the organization’s queryable QA state. Via Slack, anyone can ask:

  • “What’s the failure rate for navigation this week across all teams?”
  • “Show me regressions introduced in build 2.4.1”
  • “Which teams are seeing the most P0 bugs right now?”

This transforms the agent from a task automator into an intelligence layer. The answers require cross-team state aggregation, trend computation, and natural language interpretation – all served from persistent, indexed state that accumulates over time.

What EKS Auto Mode brings to this architecture

EKS Auto Mode launched at re:Invent 2024 with a specific promise: full Kubernetes without managing nodes. For a multi-tenant agent platform, this means:

  • Nodes appear when pods need them. Deploy a tenant namespace with an auto-filer pod. The Karpenter-based scheduler provisions a node within seconds. When the pod is deleted (tenant offboarded), the node is consolidated or terminated automatically. You never think about EC2 instances.
  • Security is not your configuration burden. Nodes run immutable Bottlerocket AMIs – read-only root filesystem, SELinux enforcing, no SSH access. Nodes rotate every 21 days automatically. For long-running agent pods, this means a graceful drain roughly every three weeks. At most one missed poll cycle.
  • Scaling is reactive to demand. During off-hours when agents are idle between polls, Auto Mode consolidates workloads onto fewer nodes. You pay for what you use.
  • GPU workloads slot in without architectural changes. Define a GPU NodePool for the ML classification service. EKS Auto Mode provisions g5 instances only when inference pods are scheduled and terminates them when done.

The multi-tenant architecture

At scale, the system would have three layers:

  1. Shared platform services: a rate limiter that prevents any single tenant from exhausting external API quotas, a connection pool manager that maintains persistent sessions to TestRail and JIRA, and a Prometheus instance collecting metrics across all tenants.
  2. Per-tenant agent namespaces: each team gets an isolated namespace containing their auto-filer pod, reporter pod, and Slack bot pod. ResourceQuotas guarantee resources. NetworkPolicies enforce that Team A’s pods cannot talk to Team B’s pods. Each namespace’s service account assumes a tenant-scoped IAM role via IRSA.
  3. Shared ML inference namespace: GPU-enabled pods running classification models that all tenants can call. This namespace has its own NodePool that scales to zero when no inference is happening.

The agent code would remain essentially the same Python that runs on Lambda today – the core decision engine (observe, dedup, decide, act) doesn’t change. What changes is the execution model: instead of being invoked per-event and destroyed, the agent runs as a long-lived async loop with persistent connections, graceful shutdown handling, and internal scheduling.

The AWS portfolio working together

The right framing isn’t “migrate off Lambda onto EKS.” It’s “use each service where it fits”:

  • Lambda remains the entry point. New teams start here. Single-team automation at $5/month with zero ops. Event-driven triggers, rapid iteration, pay-per-invocation economics.
  • Lambda + Durable Functions handles teams that need longer analysis windows or multi-step orchestration without leaving the serverless model.
  • EKS Auto Mode serves the platform layer when you need persistent multi-tenant services, cross-team intelligence, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation working together.
  • DynamoDB persists state across all layers – dedup records, bug history, trend data.
  • EventBridge orchestrates events whether the consumer is a Lambda function or a Kubernetes pod.

A team that needs 30-minute analysis windows or multi-step workflows (poll → correlate → file → notify → wait for response → update) benefits from Durable Functions without leaving serverless. You stay here until you need cross-tenant shared state or GPU – that’s the signal to evaluate Auto Mode.

“Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors.”

The intelligence moves up the stack as the organization’s needs mature. Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors.

Key takeaways

  • Start serverless: Lambda lets you validate the agentic pattern at zero operational cost. The $5/month price point removes all friction for proving the concept works. Don’t prematurely optimize for scale you don’t have.
  • Design for portability from day one: Structure your Lambda function as a pure decision engine with external state. Containerizing it means wrapping it in an async loop and adding a health endpoint. If you build Lambda functions as self-contained decision engines rather than tightly coupled to the invocation model, the transition is a one-day exercise whenever you need it.
  • The decision trigger isn’t scale – it’s workload characteristics: Don’t move because you hit 50 teams. Move when you need capabilities that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure: cross-team correlation, centralized rate limiting, GPU inference, streaming connections.
  • Multi-tenancy is an isolation problem, not a compute problem: Both Lambda (Tenant Isolation) and Kubernetes (namespaces) solve this. Choose based on what other characteristics your workload needs alongside isolation.
  • EKS Auto Mode closes the operational gap: Before Auto Mode, choosing EKS meant accepting node management overhead. Auto Mode removes that tradeoff. You get container-native execution with serverless-like operations.

The cost math

Single team on Lambda today: $3-5/month. 8-10 hours/week saved. 67x ROI. Fifty teams on EKS Auto Mode would cost approximately $200-250/month total – roughly $4-5 per team per month. Same per-team economics as Lambda, but with namespace isolation, persistent connections, GPU-ready infrastructure, centralized observability, and built-in organizational governance.

The cost-per-team barely changes. What changes is what you get for it!

What comes next?

The agentic pattern – ‘observe, decide, act’ is infrastructure-agnostic. The decision logic doesn’t care about its deployment target. What changes is what becomes possible when agents stop operating in isolation.

“The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents.”

The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents. An auto-filer agent detects a failure pattern and hands context to a root-cause agent, which traces the dependency chain across services, identifies the offending commit, and drafts a fix recommendation – all before a human sees the bug ticket. Agent-to-agent delegation, where one agent’s output becomes another’s input without human routing in between.

Beyond that: agents that build their own decision models. Today, I hand-code the dedup logic and regression detection rules. Tomorrow, the agent observes which of its filed bugs humans close as duplicates, learns from those corrections, and tightens its own classification boundaries. The system improves not because I ship better code, but because it accumulates organizational judgment over time.

The system started as a weekend project to stop filing bugs manually. It now runs in production, eliminating an entire category of manual work from QA operations. 

The infrastructure question stays the same – serverless for validation, containers for scale. But the agents running on that infrastructure are about to get significantly more capable. Teams with the platform layer ready will be the ones that can adopt those capabilities without rearchitecting.

A decision framework for scaling autonomous AI agents from AWS Lambda to EKS Auto Mode as multi-tenant workload characteristics evolve.

item.title: Perplexity’s AI agents keep working after you close the tab
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Perplexity’s new Teammates can coordinate multiple agents, remember where previous sessions left off, and keep working without another prompt. The

The post Perplexity’s AI agents keep working after you close the tab appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Perplexity’s new Teammates can coordinate multiple agents, remember where previous sessions left off, and keep working without another prompt. The challenge is keeping everything in sync, especially when agents are working at the same time, sharing project state, and operating with different permissions.

Announced Wednesday, Teammates builds on infrastructure Perplexity has spent much of the year developing. The launch puts that earlier work to use in workflows where agents can delegate tasks and continue operating across sessions.

The challenge of keeping agents stateful

When Nate Kupp, Perplexity’s vice president of infrastructure, took The New Stack inside the company’s agent sandboxes, he described the difficulty of maintaining reliable systems at that scale.

“Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build,” Kupp said, pointing to the durability and uptime requirements of operating millions of sandboxes.

“Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build”

Teammates relies on Perplexity Computer’s existing infrastructure, which separates persistent project state from individual execution environments. That allows agents to continue working on the same project without depending on a single uninterrupted session.

Shared state lives in Git

In a technical breakdown of its shared workspaces, the company described how it uses Git-backed repositories to keep project state intact across sessions. Each Computer project has its own repository, while agents work in separate sandboxes and submit their changes back to the shared project.

That gets more complicated when agents are working on the same code at once since if one agent commits its changes first, another may have to reapply its work against the latest version.

Perplexity says fewer than 2% of submissions are rejected because they’re based on outdated repository state. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds.

Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds.

Memory is handled separately through Perplexity’s Brain system, which keeps what agents have learned in dedicated repositories. That lets background agents update shared knowledge without interfering with changes to the project’s files.

Pausing and forking agents

Perplexity built SPACE around Firecracker microVMs and Btrfs snapshots, making it possible to pause, resume, or fork agent sessions without losing their saved state.

With Teammates, developers can connect tools like Slack and GitHub and set up triggers that tell agents when to act. Perplexity hasn’t said much about what happens when that work gets stuck, particularly when one agent is waiting on another or acting on information that’s already out of date.

The open permission questions

Each teammate runs in its own isolated environment and browser session, with access managed through Computer’s existing permissions and credentials handled securely through encryption. Users can also monitor progress and take control when needed.

It’s unclear how it prevents agents from accessing resources beyond their permissions when tasks are handed off. For enterprises, that uncertainty could influence how much autonomy they’re willing to give agents without requiring human approval.

Teammates is initially available on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned.

Teammates is initially available on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned.

item.title: How we review 4x more AI code without reading every line
item.dc:creator: Ankit Jain
item.description:
Do you need to read every line of AI-generated code to trust it?  Not necessarily. Instead, check five things: the

The post How we review 4x more AI code without reading every line appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Do you need to read every line of AI-generated code to trust it? 

Not necessarily. Instead, check five things: the intent behind a change, its acceptance criteria, the invariants it can’t break, the decisions made along the way, and evidence that it works.

At Aviator, that shift let the same nine engineers merge 4× more pull requests, cut median time to merge from 2.1 days to 3.4 hours, and drop reverts by 40%. A human still signs off on every PR. What changed is what that human reads.

“Decisions need a person, and a diff is the worst place to make them.”

We got the insight by sorting our own review comments. Most of what a reviewer writes on a PR is either a rule they’ve written before or a decision. Machines should check rules every time. Decisions need a person, and a diff is the worst place to make them.

The problem: Code review doesn’t scale with AI

Our code flipped from human-written with AI help to AI-generated with human help. Weekly merged PRs went from about 100 to more than 400. Our median AI-generated PR reached 640 lines, well past 400 lines, widely considered the limit where bug detection falls off.

Catching bugs was never the main point of code review anyway. In Microsoft’s 2013 study (Bacchelli & Bird), only 14% of review comments were about defects. Review is how engineers share knowledge and keep their mental model of the system current, and that’s the part worth protecting. When agents write most of the code, it’s also the part most at risk.

“Catching bugs was never the main point of code review anyway. Review is how engineers share knowledge and keep their mental model of the system current, and that’s the part worth protecting.”

Since I argued that code reviews are dead, the most common pushback I hear is, “So you just stopped reviewing?” No. We stopped reviewing the diff.

So, what didn’t work?

  • An AI reviewer. On one of my own PRs, it opened 16 of 18 threads: magic numbers, array-index React keys, a component that ran too long. One thread caught a real race condition. The two comments that mattered, both design decisions from teammates, got buried under nits.
  • A four-hour review SLA. We couldn’t add reviewers, so we added a rule. First reviews got faster, and approvals got emptier, as reviewers skimmed to hit the clock and their own work stalled.
  • A self-review skill tuned to our conventions. Its findings were far better than the generic bot’s. But it still read the diff after the code was written, and the most useful part of the exchange, what it argued about and what we decided, died in a chat window.

All three tried to read the diff better. But the diff is the least important part of code review anyway. It shows what changed, never why.

To see what review actually contained, I went back to a PR I’d reviewed in 2025. It had 14 threads. Eight came from a bot and caught one real bug. Three of my six comments were rules I’d already written on other PRs, like “Use GraphQLRetryableException so Celery retries on it.” Only two were real decisions, like “No comments extracted: should we tell the user on the PR?”

What did work: Verify intent, not lines

Code review used to do several jobs at once: catch bugs, enforce team conventions, settle design decisions, and keep everyone’s understanding of the system current. We split those jobs up and gave each one a better home.

Argue before the PR exists. Our review agent cross-examines the author’s agent, running on a different model, and writes down every disagreement. On one recent PR, the agents raised four disagreements and settled three with a stated reason. The only one left for a human was a naming call.

Capture intent and acceptance criteria. Not as an up-front spec, but captured from the coding session with the agent. Every time an engineer corrects the agent or answers its question, we create a criterion. We used to throw those away when the session ended. Intent answers why we’re making the change; acceptance criteria answer how it should behave. Intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.

“Intent answers why we’re making the change; acceptance criteria answer how it should behave. Intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.”

Codify repeated comments as invariants. We mined a year of review history in three passes: drop the noise (bot summaries, bare “LGTMs”), classify every comment as a rule, proposal, one-off fix, or question, then merge the repeats. 11,400 comments became 212 candidate rules and 64 approved invariants. Each has a scope, a verification method, provenance, and an owner.

Take “Every config change writes an audit-log entry, only when something changed.” It covers GraphQL mutations and API handlers that write config, is verified by a preview run that saves twice and reads the audit log, was mined from 23 review threads across 17 PRs, and belongs to the platform team.

A model checking every invariant on every PR is slow and not perfectly repeatable, so where possible an agent compiles invariants into ast-grep rules that run in shadow beside the model until they agree. A comment we’d left on nine PRs, “Add a timeout, this hung a worker,” is now an eight-line rule. Nineteen invariants run deterministically, in 0.3 seconds.

Prove every criterion with evidence. Each criterion becomes a scenario. An agent spins up a preview environment, drives it like a user, and records screenshots, requests, and logs. For the audit-log invariant, it saves a setting, confirms one new log entry, saves again with nothing changed, and confirms there’s still one.

That second half is exactly what a reviewer reading the diff would never check. Not every criterion needs a browser: an API contract is proven by a recorded request and response, a code rule by an ast-grep match or a file-and-line citation. Pick the cheapest proof that settles the question. A green CI check only says the tests you thought of passed.

Debate the decisions. Decisions come from three places: the coding session, the agents’ argument, and failed verification runs. The PR lists every one, where it came from, and who settled it. On a PR that added retries for failed webhook deliveries, four of five decisions were settled; the agents disagreed on whether to deduplicate retried deliveries, so a person settled that one. 

Reviewers skim what’s settled, settle what the agents couldn’t, reopen anything they’d call differently, and talk it through with the author. That conversation builds understanding of the system.

Own the rules. Engineers stop reading every line. They own the rules that check every line, and keep their understanding of the system by reading intent, evidence, and decisions.

The results

  • PRs merged per week: 4×, with the same nine engineers
  • Median time to merge: 2.1 days → 3.4 hours
  • Human threads per PR: 6.2 → 1.3
  • Reverts per 100 PRs: down 40%

Review work didn’t disappear. It moved to refining invariants, debating decisions, and improving verification. Expect the transition to hurt: month one is double work, by month two invariants catch up enough that reviews shrink, and by month three you read intent and evidence, not code.

item.title: In the software factory, engineers become process engineers
item.dc:creator: Arjun Iyer
item.description:
For most of software’s history, the scarce resource was people who could write code. Every process the industry built assumed

The post In the software factory, engineers become process engineers appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
For most of software’s history, the scarce resource was people who could write code. Every process the industry built assumed it. Sprints, code review, staging, and release trains were all designed around humans doing the work by hand.

That assumption is gone. By September, more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started with an agent’s first draft, up from 17% in March. Work is moving to machines, but the process around it hasn’t caught up.

Agents made generating code cheap and fast. For the most part, they have not yet had the same impact on shipping it. CircleCI’s 2026 delivery data showed average daily workflow runs grew 59% year over year, with the top 5% of teams up 97% and the bottom quartile showing no measurable increase. A study of one company that mandated doubling pull request output found that load per reviewer doubled and automated review overtook human review in coverage within months.

“When work gets automated in any industry, the people don’t disappear. They stop doing the work and start designing the system the work runs through.”

When work gets automated in any industry, the people don’t disappear. Their job changes. They stop doing the work and start designing the system the work runs through. Software engineers are becoming process engineers, and what they build is a software factory.

Three manufacturing lessons carry over to agents

Software is not a car plant. A factory builds the same product thousands of times, and software never ships the same change twice. But three ideas carry over, because they are about running a system where machines do the work.

The first is that people design the system, not the output. Ford’s Model T went from 12.5 hours per car to one every 93 minutes by 1914, and the workers did not get eight times faster. Engineers redesigned the line.

Second, quality gets built in at every step. Sakichi Toyoda invented a loom that stopped automatically when any thread broke, so one operator could run many machines instead of watching one. Toyota built its production system around that idea, and W. Edwards Deming spent decades telling manufacturers to stop relying on end-of-line inspection.

The third is that the slowest step sets the pace. That was Eliyahu Goldratt’s point in “The Goal.” Speed up any step other than the bottleneck, and you pile up work in front of it. Agents sped up coding, and the pile is now in review and verification.

A software factory is a network of agents

A software factory runs on many specialized agents, each good at one job, passing work to others across the lifecycle. A research agent turns usage data and customer calls into a brief, and a spec agent writes requirements with acceptance criteria. A coding agent writes the change, and a review agent reviews the change. A test agent runs the change and sends failures back, and a release agent rolls it out behind feature flags. A site reliability engineering (SRE) agent triages what breaks in production and opens the next piece of work.

Most handoffs in that loop are agent-to-agent, and that changes what a handoff is. Between humans, a handoff can be a Slack thread and some shared context. Between agents, it has to be a contract that states what gets passed, in what shape, and with what proof. A spec without acceptance criteria gives the coding agent nothing to aim at, and a change without test evidence gives the release agent nothing to trust.

“A spec without acceptance criteria gives the coding agent nothing to aim at, and a change without test evidence gives the release agent nothing to trust.”

Agent-to-agent work also fails in new ways. Errors compound, because each agent builds on the last one’s output. Agents can agree too easily, or loop forever trading the same fix back and forth. A factory of agents needs what a factory of machines needs: checks between the stations, and someone who decides where those checks go.

Software engineers become process engineers

That someone is the software engineer. The job moves from writing code to designing the system that writes, tests, and ships it. That is more technical, not less, because you are now responsible for how all the code gets made. The work comes down to four jobs, and the first is designing the flow: which agents exist, what each one owns, what runs in parallel, and what each handoff must contain.

The second is defining good. An agent can’t hit a target nobody wrote down. Specs, acceptance criteria, performance budgets, and API contracts used to live in people’s heads. Now they have to be explicit enough for a machine to check.

The third is improving the line. When an agent ships a bug, the useful question is not why the agent did that but why the line let it through. Every escaped defect is a process bug.

The fourth is placing the human gates. Humans belong where a mistake is expensive, and the call takes judgment. Line-by-line human review of every agent pull request is a craft-era habit, the factory equivalent of hand-inspecting every bolt.

“When an agent ships a bug, the useful question is not why the agent did that but why the line let it through. Every escaped defect is a process bug.”

Agents write code and fix tests. A schema migration is costly to get wrong but cheap for a machine to check, so agents run it behind hard checks. User interface (UI) copy tastes but is cheap to change, so a human reviews it after it ships. What to build and where a security boundary sits gets a human gate.

Quality gets built into every change, not inspected at the end

Most teams still run the old model of quality assurance. Changes pile up, then go through one inspection at the end: a shared staging environment and a human reviewer. That is a single test bench for the whole plant, and once agents multiply the number of changes, it becomes the bottleneck Goldratt described.

Toyoda’s loom freed the operator because it checked every thread as it ran and stopped the moment one broke. Agent-written code needs the same mechanism. In a working software factory, the test agent checks every change as it is made, the coding agent fixes what fails, and nothing moves until it passes.

That check only means something if it runs where the failure would show up. Mocks don’t count, because they tell you a change works in a world that doesn’t exist. They were a stopgap that made sense when the pace of change was slow and standing up a production-like environment for every change was hard.

So, each change gets its own environment that behaves like production, with the services, databases, and APIs it will meet after release. A human only sees the change if it hits a gate, and by then it already works, with the evidence attached.

That model needs a test station for every change, cheap enough to use on every attempt. In practice, that means an environment that comes up in seconds, deploys only what the change touched and shares everything else so that you can verify the change end to end before merge.

Guardrails belong in the line, not in the prompt

Verification catches mistakes. Guardrails stop the ones that would cost too much to catch late. Assume agents will do anything the line allows, and design the line so that everything it allows is safe.

Manufacturing calls this error-proofing. You don’t put up a sign telling workers to insert the part the right way. You build a fixture that fits only one way. For agents, an instruction in a prompt is a sign on the wall, and a permission boundary is a fixture.

So each agent holds only the access its station needs, and the coding agent never holds production credentials. Every run is isolated, so one agent’s test can’t corrupt another’s. Required checks are enforced, every release can roll back on its own, and when a check can’t run, the change stops.

A line that quietly skips a broken inspection is worse than no inspection, because everyone believes it’s working. Agent-to-agent work adds one more rule: trust doesn’t pass down the chain. A review agent approving a change shouldn’t widen what the release agent can do.

Judgment stays human, and it becomes most of the job

Factories didn’t get rid of engineers. They created industrial engineering. You can’t design a line for work you don’t understand, so the best factory builders will be engineers who know what good code, good tests, and a safe rollout look like from doing it by hand.

Some work stays off the line. The first version of something new, a strange production bug, and a design nobody has tried are bench work. They stay hands-on until they are understood well enough to standardize.

Some decisions never move to a machine: what’s worth building, what a customer means rather than what they said, when to trade speed for risk and who answers for what ships. Those were always the hard part of the job. Now they’re most of it.

The best process wins, not the best model

Agents made code cheap, and every team can reach for the same models. What separates the teams pulling ahead is the line they build around those agents, with contracts between stations, human gates where judgment matters, and verification on every change. Designing that line is now the software engineer’s job. We built Signadot to give every change its own test station, and it is a practical place to start building yours.

As AI agents automate coding, engineers become process engineers—designing the automated pipelines and human gates of the software factory.

item.title: Why AWS wants developers to stop babysitting their AI agents
item.dc:creator: Adrian Bridgwater
item.description:
AWS first introduced Kiro, its agentic, spec-driven development environment, in July 2025. It also introduced Kiro Crew in August of

The post Why AWS wants developers to stop babysitting their AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AWS first introduced Kiro, its agentic, spec-driven development environment, in July 2025. It also introduced Kiro Crew in August of this year, its persistent, open-source development workspace that remembers context. Now, to help developers juggle more complex tasks executed in parallel, AWS introduced Kiro bots on Thursday, adding persistent agent memory and delegated workflow management to the toolset. Kiro Crew already carried memory across sessions; bots give each agent its own.

Described as a “named, long-running agent that you define and customize for a specific part of your work” (such as reading new issues in a ticket queue), Kiro bots retain their own memory and start with only the tools provided to them at creation. 

The bot function also runs its own sessions (by which AWS means parallel worker sessions the bot launches and monitors), so software engineers don’t have to track them one by one or weave them together.

According to AWS, the arrival of Kiro bots heralds the shift from delegating tasks to delegating processes.

Babysitting vs. bots building better

AWS Agentic AI director of engineering Kathy Kam tells The New Stack that agents are only useful when developers can trust them to act on their own, but when a session ends, nobody owns the work anymore. 

“Developers end up as the go-between, carrying context from one session to the next. Kiro bots take that job off their plate, so developers can now spend the day deciding what’s worth building instead of babysitting sessions,” Kam says.

“Developers can now spend the day deciding what’s worth building, instead of babysitting sessions.”

Up to now, if this babysitting to carefully shepherd agents from one point to the next with more durable memory isn’t there, then the negative consequences show up pretty fast.

“You get what a lot of developers now call context rot, which can make it feel like nagging an agent to redo what you told it yesterday,” Kam explains. “It spreads fast when parallel tasks each hold their own drifting version of reality. So we gave every Kiro bot its own durable memory, with a notes [.md] file it reads and writes, and that developers can edit directly. Fix a mistake once – and it stays fixed, instead of resurfacing across every task in flight.”

Each Kiro bot works with only the tools and permissions its job needs. 

For example, a research bot can search the web and read files, but it can’t change them. A deployment bot can run deployment scripts and ask for approval before each change. A bot can ask developers for more tools, but nothing changes until the software engineer actually approves the request. Because each bot has its own memory, what the deployment bot learns about the release process does not mix with what the research bot learns. Separate lessons keep each bot aligned to its own responsibility, as judged by the developer at the outset.

Trust comes from track record

If this feels like bots and agents are developing more of their own personalities and being anthropomorphized into some sort of hierarchy, with some acting in a more senior capacity than others, then AWS’s Kam says that’s the wrong way to think about it.

“A hierarchy of agents based purely on IQ is the wrong measure. What matters is what an agent is allowed to touch, and a Kiro bot earns trust by building a track record,” underlines Kam.

“A hierarchy of agents based purely on IQ is the wrong measure. What matters is what an agent is allowed to touch, and a Kiro bot earns trust by building a track record.” 

No anthropomorphization as yet, but still, each Kiro bot has a name, an avatar, its own memory, and one ongoing chat channel where developers set its direction and come back for results. 

Behind that chat, the bot starts sessions in parallel and monitors them. It can redirect a session that drifts from the plan and combine the results when the sessions finish. If one task needs a human decision, the bot can ask the engineer while it keeps working on parts that don’t depend on an answer. Developers can set up routines in the chat, so a bot can investigate overnight build failures before the coding team even starts its day.

Yes, AWS, but what if…?

There still feels like a lot of yes, but what if… questions to surface here. What happens when bots are instructed to wait for human developer decisions, but the bot and wider agent framework already has enough institutional or historical knowledge to tell it the human doesn’t need to be involved? Doesn’t this mean the human coder should be overridden with an automation to reduce time-wasting?

“As more companies shift toward software factories, agents can end up remembering more information and context across a team than an individual developer, but that doesn’t put the agent in charge,” clarifies AWS’ Kam. “The human is still the one accountable, while the agent is responsible for executing the work. The software engineer sets how much access each Kiro bot gets for its job, so a deployment bot can require approval before every change while a research bot runs with fewer checkpoints.”

Kam further notes that a Kiro bot can “ask for more authority, but it can never take it” unmanaged. However, as already emphasized, while it waits for an answer, it keeps moving on everything that doesn’t need the human-in-the-loop.

Each Kiro bot understands its specialty, outcome, trade-offs, limits & decisions

In its official launch blog, AWS said developers using Kiro bots will find the direction given to the bot stays visible and revisable. It is set through ongoing conversation and feedback, and Kiro Crew’s learning builds within each bot. This lets the developer hand off an ongoing responsibility, not a single task. Each bot understands, for its specialty, the outcome it should aim for, the reason behind a trade-off, the limits around a change, and decisions already made. 

One Kiro bot can own issue intake while another owns release readiness, and each follows the rules set for that work. AWS noted that taken together, each developer’s “crew of bots” supports the programmer’s unique approach to development and work requirements without flattening into one generic workflow.

“Bots can’t delegate work to other bots — and that’s by design to prevent context rot and ensure Kiro bots can remain independent.”

“Bots can’t delegate work to other bots — and that’s by design to prevent context rot and ensure Kiro bots can remain independent,” highlights Kam. “A Kiro bot splits big jobs across its own parallel workstreams and pulls the results into one recommendation. Developers stay the one defining each’s boundaries and connecting Kiro bots to each other, so no decision that you want to provide input on moves between them without you being involved.”

AWS also explained that over time, a developer’s bot crew “reflects how you actually develop”, because each bot carries the requirements and boundaries for its part of the work needed. The software engineer still decides how those processes change and where judgment belongs.

To get started, AWS has encouraged developers to open the bots workspace in the Kiro Crew sidebar, add a bot, and choose the default or a custom agent as its base. A custom agent supplies the prompt, model, tools, and skills, so users can build on a setup they already use without changing existing chats. In summary, with all the autonomy swirling around here, we might suggest that AWS isn’t asking developers to give up the steering wheel, but perhaps it’s asking them to sit further away from the passenger seat when AI is doing the driving.

AWS’s new Kiro bots keep their own memory and run parallel agent sessions. The promise: developers stop ferrying context and decide what to build.

item.title: AI agents are getting more complex. Developers shouldn’t have to babysit them.
item.dc:creator: Kimberly Fessel
item.description:
What if your coding agent could catch its own mistakes before you ever reviewed its work?  A few years ago,

The post AI agents are getting more complex. Developers shouldn’t have to babysit them. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
What if your coding agent could catch its own mistakes before you ever reviewed its work? 

A few years ago, AI hallucinations seemed to be everywhere. (Just how many r’s are there in strawberry?) Early AI tools required extensive human oversight, with developers constantly reviewing code and checking for errors. But today, advances in AI agent engineering are making self-correction a reality. 

Through harness engineering, teams can equip their agents with automated tests, feedback loops, and guardrails that help them identify and correct mistakes before humans review them.

Recommended Download: Thoughtworks’ Technology Radar, Volume 35

As a result, agents can tackle longer-running tasks with less intervention, while multiple agents work in parallel without stepping on each other’s toes.

Our guest on the latest episode of The New Stack podcast, Vanitha Kumar, principal technologist at Thoughtworks, explains that harness engineering has two parts.

Kumar tells TNS: “Do it right the first time and also self-correct when you have done it for the first time.” 

The payoff, according to Kumar, is that you no longer have to “babysit and watch your agent do the work.”

Enabling one agent to act autonomously is different from managing hundreds of them across an entire organization. That’s where AI factories come in. Kumar compares their emergence to the rise of Kubernetes, which helped developers abstract away the complexity of microservice infrastructure. AI factories help teams set up standardized infrastructure for model selection, workload management, and cost optimization. As she puts it, “The best way to build a platform is [to] make it easy to do the right thing.”

Greater agent autonomy frees up developer time, but it also means agents require access to more data, systems, and tools, which potentially introduce additional security vulnerabilities. Some organizations are delaying AI adoption to avoid exposing their systems to extra security risks. 

Harness guardrails may help alleviate these concerns by restricting access to tooling, enforcing test environments, and requiring human approval for sensitive changes. 

When asked about next year’s AI trends, Kumar makes this prediction: “Security is going to be a big topic. Not even one year out.”

She also discusses Thoughtworks’ Technology Radar, Volume 35, released on November 4, 2026. The report emphasizes AI, harness engineering, emerging agent practices, and, perhaps surprisingly, established engineering practices that are suddenly more important. For example, penetration testing and path-to-production understanding appear in the report, which Kumar explains as “… old things that are making a comeback because they now have more added weight because of AI.”

item.title: Cognition turned an open model into a coding beast. But it won’t release the weights.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Cognition built its newest coding model on a foundation that anyone can download, yet the company is keeping its own

The post Cognition turned an open model into a coding beast. But it won’t release the weights. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Cognition built its newest coding model on a foundation that anyone can download, yet the company is keeping its own finished version locked away.

Released Wednesday, SWE-2 Flash costs one-fifth as much as Cognition’s larger SWE-2 model and generates tokens roughly three times faster, according to the company. Built on Thinking Machines Lab’s open weight Inkling-Small, the new model comes with a catch: Cognition is keeping its weights private, citing cybersecurity concerns.

Inkling-Small is a 276-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 12 billion active parameters that Thinking Machines Lab, the startup led by co-founder and CEO Mira Murati, released on July 30 under an Apache 2.0 license, which means anyone can pull the weights from Hugging Face and build on them.

“a practical way to turn a weak open base into a usable agent model,”

Cognition says the bulk of its performance gains came from adding a mid-training stage before reinforcement learning, and the numbers it published are striking — on Terminal-Bench 4.0, Flash scored 20% against Inkling-Small’s 0.9%, and its FrontierCode 2.0 score climbed from the base model’s 3.2% to 24%, narrowly edging out SWE-2’s 23.8%.

CultOfAI, an AI commentary account on X, calls mid-training “a practical way to turn a weak open base into a usable agent model,” though the same account cautions that the figures are Cognition’s own rather than independently verified.

Cheaper, faster, still trailing

Flash doesn’t keep pace with the larger model on every test, coming within a hair on SWE-Bench Pro v2 Hard at 89.9% to SWE-2’s 90.6% but trailing on DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 4.0, while competitors including Claude Haiku 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outscore it on several benchmarks.

Open base, private weights

Building on a model released under Apache 2.0, one of the more permissive open source licenses, doesn’t obligate Cognition to open its own work, since the license lets developers modify and commercialize derivatives without sharing their changes — so keeping SWE-2 Flash’s weights private sits well within the company’s rights even as it cuts against the spirit of the base it borrowed.

The decision caught the attention of David Hendrickson, CEO of GenerAIte Solutions, who praised Cognition for turning Inkling-Small into a “coding beast” but pointed out on X that “the improved weights aren’t public.”

His observation comes as open-weight models close the performance gap with proprietary alternatives and become serious contenders for coding platforms. Cognition’s decision to keep its improved model private contrasts with that trend.

Cognition says it’s building a program to share the weights with select industry partners and research labs that could inspect, fine-tune, and run the model on their own infrastructure, an arrangement likely to appeal to enterprises and governments wary of sensitive code leaving their systems.

More details are coming in the next few weeks, the company says, and for now it remains unclear who will qualify, what restrictions they’ll face, or whether they’ll be allowed to share models built on SWE-2 Flash.

Cybersecurity drives the lockdown

Cybersecurity is central to Cognition’s decision to restrict the weights. The company included cybersecurity tasks in Flash’s training, raising its ExploitBench score from Inkling-Small’s 11.3% to 34.8%. That’s a significant improvement, although the benchmark doesn’t establish how the model would perform in real-world attacks or whether releasing its weights would increase the risk of misuse.

Cognition points to a rise in AI-enabled cyberattacks as justification for limiting access.

The concern is that capabilities used to find and investigate vulnerabilities could just as easily help attackers. Cognition points to a rise in AI-enabled cyberattacks as justification for limiting access. Similar challenges are trending across the industry; AI tools can now identify tens of thousands of potential vulnerabilities in open-source projects faster than maintainers can investigate and fix them.

American model, limited access

Cognition describes SWE-2 Flash as a fully American coding model and claims it beats every American open-weight model on leading evaluations, including models three times its size, a qualification that carries weight because the company’s own benchmark table shows models built outside the United States, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash among them, outscoring Flash on several tests.

Developers can try SWE-2 Flash through Devin Desktop and CLI, and the model is free through November 30.

item.title: Meta’s best AI model now trains the one most of its users get
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Starting on Friday, everyone using Meta’s Muse agent and Meta AI gets new models the company trained using Muse Wonder,

The post Meta’s best AI model now trains the one most of its users get appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Starting on Friday, everyone using Meta’s Muse agent and Meta AI gets new models the company trained using Muse Wonder, its frontier model. Subscribers still get Wonder itself for harder tasks.

Meta hasn’t named the new models, though we can assume their codenames don’t involve fruits. The company calls them “specialized” versions of its existing ones that were “trained using Muse Wonder.” They also come with two features the company first introduced with Wonder: Active Memory and Active Focus.

Meta originally launched Wonder and the more capable Wonder Full on Oct. 12. Wonder is currently available through the Meta Model API and in Muse Code, the company’s coding agent, while Wonder Full is limited to Muse Code’s two most expensive plans.

Wonder-trained models for everyone

Muse, Meta’s personal agent app, launched in September on the smaller Muse Spark model and became somewhat of a breakout hit for Meta and introduced consumers to the idea of personal agents.

Unlike many personal agents, Muse has a free tier, giving it a far lower barrier of entry than OpenAI’s Dots or Anthropic’s Duet, which are only available to subscribers on those vendors’ highest pricing tiers.

What’s maybe most interesting here from a technical perspective is that Meta didn’t simply develop a smaller, general-purpose version of Wonder.

Instead, the company stresses that it trained the new models on the behaviors that matter in a consumer app like Muse. That means the agents have to decide when to work on their own and when to check with the user, for example, and be able to take corrections in the middle of a task without losing track.

Using a large model to train smaller ones is obviously a common way for AI labs to get frontier behavior into products at consumer scale, but Meta sadly hasn’t detailed its method.

It’s also worth noting that Meta is tuning those models for very specific use cases.

A personal agent need to be able to a restaurant table and manage a user’s inbox, but the model that powers that agent doesn’t need to know everything a frontier model knows. But it does need to remember what a user said a week ago, and know how to keep going when a website breaks halfway through a booking.

That’s where features like Active Memory and Active Focus come in.

“Active Memory”

Active Memory helps the models remember details and take them from earlier conversations into new ones.

As Meta writes in its announcement, “We’ve trained our models to recognize what type of information is temporary versus permanent, to reason across time, and to distinguish between what is still relevant and what has become stale.”

On Meta’s internal evaluation, the new models in Muse correctly use critical context in 90% of tasks, up from 76% for the previous model.

“Active Focus”

Active Focus is focused on keeping the models working on a task when something goes awry.

“We’ve trained our models on a variety of bottlenecks reflective of the real world,” Meta writes, “so that they can try harder, recover, or find alternatives on your behalf.” I

In Muse, the company reports a 67% improvement in finishing routine tasks when these new models run into unexpected problems, but it didn’t share the baseline.

Meta says the models are also better at deciding when to work on their own and when to check with the user, and they handle corrections in the middle of a task.

Two tiers of models

On the API, Wonder costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, while Muse also has a free tier and Meta AI runs inside WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and Messenger.

Training lighther-weight models with Wonder is likely a cheaper way to reach that many users than serving Wonder itself to all of them.

Meta trained new models using its frontier Muse Wonder model and is shipping them to all Muse and Meta AI users today, while keeping Wonder itself for harder subscriber tasks.

item.title: “Most apps never make it off localhost”: Cursor takes on Lovable and Replit with fully managed app deployment
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
AI coding agents have certainly made it easier to transform an idea into a working application. However, getting that application

The post “Most apps never make it off localhost”: Cursor takes on Lovable and Replit with fully managed app deployment appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI coding agents have certainly made it easier to transform an idea into a working application. However, getting that application off a local machine and into the hands of real users remains a hurdle, requiring essential infrastructure steps spanning everything from hosting and database provisioning, to critical security checks.

Cursor, the AI coding platform acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX for $60 billion back in August, acknowledged the problem in an X post published on Thursday.

“Agents have made it easier to write code, but most apps never make it off localhost,” the company notes.

To address this, Cursor is introducing new app-building and deployment functionality, designed to take AI-generated applications from development to a live, shareable URL, without users having to even think about the underlying infrastructure themselves.

“Agents have made it easier to write code, but most apps never make it off localhost.”

Built on cloud agents

The new feature is built around cloud agents, which Cursor introduced last year as a way for developers to run multiple AI coding agents remotely without having to keep their laptops engaged. At the time, the company highlighted their ability to fix bugs, handle smaller coding tasks and implement some complex features.

With this latest update, those same agents can now take applications all the way through to deployment, handling the important steps needed to make them accessible to other users. The functionality is only available through cloud agents, though, which means it can’t be used with agents running locally.

Users start by describing the application they want to build in natural language, with Cursor managing the code generation and development process as usual.

From there, the agent creates the application and sets up the underlying project, including the necessary components to get it running.

Once the application is ready, users can preview the result before deciding whether to hit publish.

Publishing makes the application accessible through a live URL, allowing users to share it with colleagues or other users without having to configure hosting themselves.

It’s worth noting that there are two ways to get started. Users building an application from scratch will automatically have a new repository created on Cursor Origin, the company’s Git-based code-hosting platform launched in August as an agent-centric alternative to GitHub.

Alternatively, users can deploy applications from an existing GitHub repository. This means developers who already have an application under development can use Cursor’s cloud agents to prepare and publish it, without having to move their code to Origin or set up deployment infrastructure manually.

Judging by Cursor’s own examples, the feature seemingly targets employees who need to create internal business applications, such as sales dashboards, onboarding programs, customer presentations and developer portals. So in that regard, it could prove a boon for non-developers who have an idea for a tool but lack the technical nous to get it running themselves.

Of course, there’s nothing restricting the feature to business applications. An aspiring vibe coder could just as easily create a neighbourhood football league tracker or interactive family holiday planner. And because individual subscribers can publish apps publicly, those creations can be shared with anyone who has the link.

Under the hood: hosting, databases and security

Cursor had actually begun closing this gap, when in August it introduced the ability to preview cloud-agent projects and publish them to a live URL. However, users still needed to connect their own Vercel accounts.

The latest release removes that requirement while introducing various new smarts to the mix.

Behind the scenes, Cursor now takes care of several infrastructure requirements, including hosting, databases, and authentication.

For hosting, Cursor automatically creates a dedicated account for each team or individual subscriber, isolated from other customers. While Cursor’s announcement doesn’t identify the underlying hosting provider, Vercel revealed in a separate response on X that the new functionality is built on its Vercel for Platforms infrastructure. This basically allows users to deploy applications without having to create their own Vercel accounts or configure hosting themselves.

If an application needs a database, Cursor provisions one using PostgreSQL, while private and team applications are protected by Cursor’s existing sign-in system. Individual subscribers can also make their apps publicly accessible.

Applications can connect to external services, such as company databases or data warehouses, with users supplying the necessary credentials. Cursor says these secrets are managed separately, meaning the AI agent never sees their actual values.

Then there’s the thorny issue of security. When users choose to publish an application, Cursor says it runs “a series of deterministic and agentic security checks” before allowing it to go live. These include mandatory checks for exposed credentials, secrets and sensitive files, alongside an AI-powered review intended to identify more serious vulnerabilities.

However, it’s unclear how reliably these automated checks can identify more complex problems, such as incorrectly configured database permissions or application-level access controls. This is an important consideration for organisations contemplating connecting AI-generated applications to sensitive internal systems, where additional security scrutiny would still be advisable.

There is precedent for such concerns, too. In May last year, Semafor reported that two Replit employees examined 1,645 Lovable-built applications and discovered that 170 of them exposed sensitive information. The problems involved incorrectly configured database permissions, highlighting the difficulties of securing applications created through AI tools. Lovable says it subsequently introduced further security checks to identify potential vulnerabilities before applications are published.

Cursor moves onto Lovable and Replit’s turf

Of course, Cursor is entering territory already occupied by the likes of Lovable and Replit, which allow users to create and publish applications through natural-language prompts.

While Cursor’s latest announcement emphasizes internal business tools, Lovable and Replit have traditionally appealed to a broader audience of aspiring application creators. Still, the overlap is clear, and Cursor’s move into deployment has already caught the attention of developers.

“Cursor just came for the localhost graveyard.”

One software engineer writes on X that “cursor just came for the localhost graveyard,” riffing on Cursor’s own messaging about AI-generated applications that never make it beyond local development.

There’s also an interesting overlap with Grok Build, particularly given SpaceX’s acquisition of Cursor in August.

SpaceXAI introduced Grok’s Build Mode in July, before expanding it to all Grok plans the following month. The feature allows users to create apps, games and websites directly inside a Grok conversation, then publish them to shareable grok.me links.

That bears something of a resemblance to Cursor’s latest offering, although Cursor is approaching it through its established coding environment and cloud agents, and with a stronger emphasis on business applications and managed infrastructure.

The overlap hasn’t gone unnoticed though. One X user responded to Cursor’s announcement by asking, “so cursor is now properly replacing grok build?”

There’s no indication that Grok Build is being replaced, but the two offerings now cover some notably similar ground, raising questions about how SpaceXAI intends to distinguish them going forward.

For those wanting to check out Cursor’s new functionality, it’s available on all paid Cursor plans with cloud agents enabled.

With deployment increasingly becoming part of the AI coding experience, Cursor’s latest move could put further pressure on dedicated app-building platforms as the distinction between tools aimed at professional developers and those targeting aspiring vibe coders continues to narrow.

The post “Most apps never make it off localhost”: Cursor takes on Lovable and Replit with fully managed app deployment appeared first on The New Stack.
Cursor no longer stops at writing code. Its agents now spin up databases, configure logins and hosting, and check for security flaws before apps go live.

item.title: Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Google wants to emulate one of its biggest ever open-source success stories, donating three core AI agent infrastructure projects to

The post Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google wants to emulate one of its biggest ever open-source success stories, donating three core AI agent infrastructure projects to a neutral foundation in the hope they become industry standards, just as Kubernetes did for containers.

In a blog post published on Thursday, Drew Bradstock, VP of product management, Kubernetes and orchestration at Google, confirmed that the company is donating gVisor, Agent Substrate, and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF).

The move comes amid growing concerns about the security of autonomous AI agents, particularly their ability to execute code and interact with external systems. In July, models undergoing a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI escaped their restricted environment and breached Hugging Face’s production infrastructure, highlighting the challenges of keeping increasingly capable agents contained.

“We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes.”

Bradstock, for his part, argues that addressing such security risks, while making agents more economical to run and train, requires closer cooperation across the various facets of the underlying software and hardware infrastructure. And he believes that putting its technologies under neutral governance could encourage the kind of industry-wide participation that helped Kubernetes become ubiquitous.

“We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes,” Bradstock writes.

Why Google’s giving away gVisor

By way of a brief recap, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018 to improve container security. As The New Stack explained later that year, the technology uses a lightweight kernel running in user space to intercept application system calls, providing an additional layer of isolation between containers and the underlying host operating system. This makes it particularly useful for running untrusted code, including code generated by AI agents.

The technology is used by major AI companies, including Anthropic, which runs code generated by Claude inside gVisor containers on its web platform; and OpenAI, which uses it to isolate code execution. In a security report published just on Wednesday, OpenAI cited sandboxes such as gVisor and Firecracker as important for limiting the damage from exploited Linux kernel vulnerabilities.

The donation itself has been in the works for several weeks. The CNCF accepted gVisor’s application in late September, with Google publicly announcing its plans a few days later. The project’s onboarding process began last week, ahead of Thursday’s broader announcement incorporating all three projects.

In its original October announcement, gVisor contributors and Google software engineers Etienne Perot and Jing Chen sought to reassure users that the company remained committed to the technology. With demand for affordable, secure sandboxes growing, they argued that independent governance could encourage wider participation and adoption, both within Google and beyond.

“We (the gVisor contributors at Google) have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google, in a similar manner as what has happened with Kubernetes,” they wrote at the time.

“We have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google.”

Agent Substrate addresses a different challenge: how to run large numbers of autonomous agents without wasting computing resources while they sit idle. As The New Stack reported in July, the project introduces an additional runtime layer on top of Kubernetes, allowing agents to be suspended when inactive and resumed when needed, without repeatedly creating and destroying Kubernetes Pods. It does this by separating an agent’s persistent state from the computing resources executing it, with gVisor providing one of the available options for securely isolating that execution.

As part of the announcement this week, Google officially released Agent Substrate 1.0 and made it generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).

OpenRL, meanwhile, focuses on reinforcement learning, allowing developers to fine-tune AI models on their own Kubernetes infrastructure. Publicly introduced in June, the project coordinates the training and evaluation processes used to improve models. It also integrates with Agent Substrate, allowing training exercises to run inside isolated environments that can be secured using gVisor.

Collectively, the three projects address the execution, security and training requirements of autonomous AI agents.

Going vendor neutral

The move to CNCF governance should also change how gVisor is developed and maintained. In their October announcement, Perot and Chen outlined plans to move the project’s development and testing infrastructure outside Google, give external maintainers permission to merge code, and introduce a governance model that prevents any single company from exercising unilateral control.

Notably, in the project’s CNCF application submitted through GitHub in September, Perot identified a divide among gVisor’s existing adopters. At one end are major technology companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, which can invest in adapting the technology to their needs; at the other are specialist startups whose businesses depend heavily on secure code execution. The opportunity, Perot suggested, lies in reaching the much broader market between those two camps.

Such companies “don’t have the resources to invest specifically into security but would happily adopt an off-the-shelf, widely-available sandboxing runtime,” Perot wrote in the application.

There’s also the question of why more cloud providers haven’t integrated gVisor into their commercial offerings. In their October announcement, Perot and Chen noted that Google, DigitalOcean and Modal were among the few providers selling general-purpose computing services powered by gVisor, despite evidence that customers were already installing the technology themselves on competing cloud platforms. The engineers suggested that concerns about Google’s control of the project could explain the discrepancy.

“The remaining explanation of the lack of direct integration is likely the project’s (pre-donation) governance risk,” they wrote.

But perhaps the most interesting obstacle concerns the Linux kernel itself. Google and other companies using gVisor maintain their own kernel modifications to improve its performance, particularly for I/O-intensive applications. Those improvements aren’t universally available, potentially leaving other users with slower execution environments.

Bradstock attributes the difficulty in getting those improvements incorporated into the mainline Linux kernel to gVisor’s hitherto Google-centric credentials.

“Upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor.”

“Upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor,” Bradstock writes.

There is also documented resistance to at least one earlier gVisor-related kernel proposal on technical grounds. As LWN reported in 2022, Linux kernel maintainers raised security and design concerns about a proposed performance improvement, including questions about its usefulness beyond gVisor.

While such interactions don’t focus on Google’s ownership as a reason for the objections, it’s clear that moving to CNCF governance should go some distance toward addressing concerns about single-vendor control.

And for Google, that effort now extends beyond gVisor. With Agent Substrate and OpenRL also moving to the CNCF, the company is hoping to establish a common foundation for autonomous agents.

“Vendor-neutral ownership lets cloud providers, hardware vendors, and independent software companies participate in the future growth of agentic workloads equally,” Bradstock writes.

The post Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI appeared first on The New Stack.
The sandbox heads to the CNCF alongside Agent Substrate and OpenRL, as Google bets neutral governance can make its AI agent stack an industry standard.

item.title: HumanLayer just got acquired by Factory. But it gave users a way out first.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Factory has acquired HumanLayer, its third AI coding startup in less than a month, as it works to fold more

The post HumanLayer just got acquired by Factory. But it gave users a way out first. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Factory has acquired HumanLayer, its third AI coding startup in less than a month, as it works to fold more of the software engineering lifecycle into a single autonomous platform. The deal deepens Factory’s bench, but it also leaves existing HumanLayer users weighing what to do with the tools they already depend on.

Announced Wednesday, the acquisition brings HumanLayer founders Dex Horthy and Kyle Mistele to Factory, along with technology for coordinating multiple coding agents and collaborating on their work. It arrives as demand for agentic coding tools climbs at a pace few enterprise products ever see, pushing the companies building them to consolidate fast.

“It arrives as demand for agentic coding tools climbs at a pace few enterprise products ever see…”

Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg welcomes the pair on X, writing that he has “been a huge fan of @dexhorthy and @0xblacklight for a while now,” and calling them two of the most ambitious polymaths he has met.

What happens to users

The founders write in their announcement that Factory will “also be refunding paying customers for the last several months,” though neither company has set a shutdown date for HumanLayer’s hosted service or said which features will carry over.

For users who would rather not migrate, HumanLayer open-sourced its core software under Apache 2.0 on October 23, an escape hatch that still comes with caveats. Some processes require third-party API keys even when those integrations go unused, a rough edge the company says it is working to remove as it makes the software easier to deploy on its own.

Three deals, four weeks

HumanLayer caps a quick run of deals that map Factory’s priorities. On October 9, Factory acquired Mentlio, a Y Combinator startup focused on making coding agents more cost-efficient through model routing, context compression and spending analysis.

Three weeks later, on October 30, it acquired Typedef, which builds tools for understanding the relationships across data models, pipelines and dashboards, technology Factory plans to point at enterprise data migrations and refactoring.

HumanLayer brings collaboration to that mix, with multiplayer tasks, shared editing of agent-generated plans and documents, and live streaming of code changes during agent sessions. Factory says those capabilities will begin arriving over the coming weeks without naming specific release dates, and it has not disclosed the purchase price for any of the three deals.

Inside Factory’s agent playbook

Factory’s coding agents, known as Droids, handle everything from planning and writing code to testing and maintenance. HumanLayer’s founders have focused on what happens when teams run multiple coding agents at once, including managing context, coordinating tasks, and reviewing results.

Factory’s coding agents, known as Droids, handle everything from planning and writing code to testing and maintenance.

Horthy and Mistele also helped popularize the Research/Plan/Implement workflow, which breaks coding tasks into separate stages. Their work fits Factory’s effort to bring more of the development process into one platform. Mentlio helps control agent costs, Typedef adds enterprise data capabilities, and HumanLayer brings tools for collaboration.

The standalone question

But HumanLayer users still don’t know whether the hosted service will continue beyond the transition, what they’ll pay if they move to Factory, or which features they’ll be able to keep. The open-source version gives them another option, although they’ll have to host and maintain it themselves. For now, it’s unclear how much of HumanLayer will remain available as a standalone product.

“HumanLayer users still don’t know whether the hosted service will continue beyond the transition, what they’ll pay if they move to Factory, or which features they’ll be able to keep.”
